chunks: Muhammad ibn Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥusain narrated to me from al-Ḥasan ibn ‘Ali ibn Mahziyār, from his father, from al-Ḥasan ibn Sa‘īd, from Zur‘ah ibn Muḥammad al-Ḥaḍrami, from al-Mufaḍḍal ibn ‘Umar, who said:

Abū ‘Abdillāh (peace be upon him) said: ‘Going to the Ziyārah is better than not going, and not going is better than going.’ I said, ‘You broke my back!’ He said, ‘By Allāh, one of you goes to the grave of his father anguished and grieved, but you come to him (the Imam) with your own selves [dressed in fine clothes]. No! [It is better not to go] unless you go disheveled and covered with dust.’
ai.seo_question: What is the proper etiquette and demeanor for visiting the Imams according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Imam al-Ṣādiq (a.s.) uses the relatable experience of visiting one's own father to illustrate the proper spiritual demeanor for Ziyārah, contrasting the casual, grief-stricken humility of family visits with the often overly formal or well-groomed appearance of visitors to the Imams. He prescribes appearing 'shu‘thān ghubran' (disheveled and dusty) not merely as physical neglect, but as an outward manifestation of inner humility, awe, and the profound emotional weight of standing before the sacred presence. This hadith, found in Ibn Qulawayh’s *Kāmil al-Ziyārāt*, underscores the Shia emphasis on *khushū‘* (devotional humility) as the core etiquette of pilgrimage to the shrines.
